lines.text: A hill outside ancient Rome, a fisherman's tomb, and the smallest country on Earth. This is the story of Vatican City and its popes.
It begins with Peter, a fisherman from Galilee who followed Jesus. Tradition says he died in Rome and was buried on the Vatican hill.
From the seven hundreds the popes ruled much of central Italy as kings, the Papal States, until Italy was united in 1870.
Julius the Second, the warrior pope, would begin a new Saint Peter's and set Michelangelo and Raphael to work.
In the 1470s the Sistine Chapel was built, the hall where cardinals still gather to elect a pope.
Soon after, Pope Sixtus the Fourth formally founded the Vatican Library, keeper of some of the oldest copies of the Bible.
In 1506 the Swiss Guard arrived, Catholic soldiers from Switzerland in famous striped uniforms, guarding the pope ever since.
That same year work began on the new Saint Peter's, over Peter's tomb. Bramante, Michelangelo and Bernini all shaped it, crowned by a great dome.
Julius also began the collections that grew into the Vatican Museums.
In the pope's rooms Raphael painted The School of Athens, the thinkers of ancient Greece gathered around Plato and Aristotle.
And in 1512 Michelangelo finished the Sistine ceiling, four years of work that brought Genesis to life, with the creation of Adam at its heart.
Karol Wojtyla, born in Poland, would one day become Pope John Paul the Second and travel the whole world.
In 1929 Vatican City was born, a country of its own inside Rome, the smallest in the world.
It was the Lateran Treaty with Italy that made it so, settling the long quarrel since the loss of the Papal States.
Jorge Mario Bergoglio of Buenos Aires would become Pope Francis, the first from the Americas, a voice for the poor and for migrants.
Robert Prevost, born in the United States, would one day succeed him as Leo the Fourteenth.
From 1962 bishops from around the world met in the Second Vatican Council, bringing the Mass into local languages and opening the Church to other faiths.
On Easter Monday 2025 Pope Francis died, and he was buried in the Roman basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore.
In May the cardinals met in the Sistine Chapel, and elected Leo the Fourteenth, the first pope from the United States.
From a fisherman's grave to a living state, Peter's hill still draws the world to Rome.
